cycle_time.insight: The 53-day gap between median cycle time (72.9 days) and P85 (126.0 days) — where the slowest 15% of items take 73% longer than the median — signals poor predictability; a stakeholder planning on the median will be wrong one time in six. The improving trend (-6.22 days/week) is encouraging but Bugs complete nearly 2.4× faster (median 31.7 days) than Product Backlog Items (median 75.0 days), suggesting that work type or the path through the review and release gates differs significantly by item type.
evidence: Median 72.9 days, P85 126.0 days — 53-day spread, 73% above median at the 85th percentile
Bugs median 31.7 days vs PBIs median 75.0 days — 2.4× difference
Trend slope -6.22 days/week with 7 items above P85 in the 6-month window
cycle_time.watch_out: Monitor whether the improving trend persists once the Feb 16 batch-completion anomaly ages out of the sample; if cycle time plateaus around 65-70 days, the remaining constraint is likely structural (review or release cadence) rather than process improvement.

lead_time.insight: A median lead time of 39.1 days (P85 58.2 days) gives stakeholders a reasonable 5–8 week planning horizon for most requests, and the strong improving trend (-11.61 days/week) is the fastest-improving metric in the dataset. Bugs and PBIs have nearly identical median lead times (36.2 vs 36.0 days), indicating that from a customer's perspective, the speed of bug resolution and feature delivery is currently equivalent.
evidence: Median lead time 39.1 days, P85 58.2 days — only 49% above median, more predictable than cycle time
Trend slope -11.61 days/week — strongest improving signal across all metrics
Bugs median 36.2 days, PBIs median 36.0 days — effectively equal
lead_time.watch_out: The lead time sample (30 items) is smaller than the cycle time sample (48 items) and the two appear to cover partially different populations; the median lead time (39.1 days) being lower than median cycle time (72.9 days) suggests items without a board entry in 'New' are included only in cycle time — interpret type-by-type comparisons across the two metrics with caution.

throughput.insight: At 1.8 items per week on average — with 17 of 26 weeks recording zero completions — throughput is too low and too variable for reliable forecasting. The two spike weeks (45 items on Feb 16 and 13 items on Apr 13) account for the majority of all completions and suggest delivery is happening in planned batches rather than a continuous pull. The 'worsening' trend slope (-1.33/week) is largely an artefact of regressing from the Feb 16 spike; recent weeks (5 and 7 completions in late July and early August) are a more honest signal of current capacity.
evidence: 17 of 26 weeks had zero completions
Feb 16 alone: 45 completions (57% of all completions in the first 10 weeks of the window)
Recent pattern: 5 completions week of Jul 27, 7 completions week of Aug 3 — more representative of current state
throughput.watch_out: If the 5–7 completions/week pattern seen in late July and early August is sustained through September, the trend slope will turn positive; treat the current 'worsening' label as misleading until 3–4 more weeks of clean data are available.

time_in_columns.insight: Ready for release is the primary bottleneck with a mean dwell of 344 hours (85% above the cross-column average), indicating that work regularly waits for deployment after it is functionally complete. In Review is the second-largest accumulator with a mean of 212.6 hours and a median of 184 hours — the near-equal mean and median confirm this is a systemic capacity problem rather than a few outliers. External Review shows extreme skew (mean 206.7h vs median 41.9h), meaning a small number of items are stuck waiting for external parties for weeks.
evidence: Ready for release: mean 344.4h, ratio 1.85× average — identified bottleneck
In Review: mean 212.6h, median 184.0h — skew ratio near 1, confirming systemic not outlier-driven delay
External Review: mean 206.7h but median only 41.9h — extreme right tail from a few stuck items
time_in_columns.watch_out: Addressing the Ready for release bottleneck (e.g. more frequent release cadence or automated deployment) could shorten cycle time by an estimated 1–2 weeks for most items; confirm whether the release gate is a team-owned constraint or depends on an external platform team.

flow_efficiency.insight: A median flow efficiency of 76.6% appears healthy at face value, but 27 of 106 items (25.5%) sit below 20% efficiency — meaning a quarter of all work spends more than 80% of its total time waiting rather than being actively worked. The bimodal signal (P85 at 100%, many items at very low efficiency) points to two distinct populations: items that flow end-to-end with little wait, and items that get stranded in External Review or Ready for release for extended periods.
evidence: Median efficiency 76.6% — apparently healthy
27 of 106 items (25.5%) below 20% efficiency — significant low tail
P85 at 100% — at least 15% of items have near-zero wait time, likely short or direct-path items
flow_efficiency.watch_out: The high median may be masking structural problems for items that pass through External Review or become blocked; segment efficiency by item type and by whether items visited External Review or Ready for release to identify which paths are creating the low tail.

work_start_efficiency.insight: With a median wait of 6.2 days before development starts and a mean work-start efficiency of 76.6% (across 14 items), the team appears to pick up committed work relatively promptly — no items waited more than half their total time before reaching In Development. This is one of the stronger signals in the dataset and suggests prioritisation and queue management at the Ready for Dev stage is functioning adequately under normal conditions.
evidence: Median wait before development: 6.2 days
Mean work-start efficiency: 76.6%; median: 77.4%
0 of 14 items fell below 50% efficiency before starting development
work_start_efficiency.watch_out: The sample is very small (14 items); note also that Ready for Dev currently holds 7 items against a WIP limit of 5 — this queue violation may lengthen the wait before development starts for new items arriving now.

wip.insight: Current WIP of 19 items is consistent with the observed cycle time via Little's Law (19 ÷ 1.8/week ≈ 10.6 weeks = 74 days, matching the observed median of 72.9 days), confirming the system is behaving predictably. However, the composition is concerning: 47% of current WIP (9 items) are bugs, and Ready for Dev holds 7 items against a WIP limit of 5 — the only active WIP limit violation — indicating the team is queuing more work than it can start.
evidence: WIP 19, throughput 1.8/week → predicted cycle time 10.6 weeks (actual median 10.4 weeks — Little's Law confirmed)
9 of 19 WIP items are bugs (47.4%)
Ready for Dev: 7 items vs WIP limit of 5 — only active column-level violation
wip.watch_out: If bugs continue arriving at current rates while PBI completions stall, the bug share of WIP will exceed 50%, effectively making the team a bug-fixing team with little remaining capacity for feature delivery.

wip_over_time.insight: WIP has broadly decreased from a high of 73 (mid-February) to a current 18–19, driven primarily by the Feb 16 mass completion event and subsequent lower intake. The recent uptick — from a low of 7 (Jul 19) to 18 (Aug 2) in six weeks — coincides with the late-July bug creation spike (13 bugs in 2 weeks) and suggests the improving WIP trend may be reversing.
evidence: Peak WIP: 73 (Feb 15); current: 19 — a 74% reduction overall
Mean WIP: 29.9; overall trend slope: -2.13/week
WIP rising again: 7 (Jul 19) → 12 (Jul 26) → 18 (Aug 2) — a 157% increase in 3 weeks
wip_over_time.watch_out: Monitor closely over the next 3 weeks: if WIP continues rising above 20 without a corresponding increase in completions, the team risks returning to the high-WIP / slow-cycle-time regime seen in February and March.

wip_age_distribution.insight: Of 19 active items, 6 (31.6%) are older than 30 days — a significant proportion given a median cycle time of ~73 days. Items in the 8–14 day band (6 items) likely represent healthy recently started work, but the 6 items older than 30 days are already approaching or exceeding the historical median without completing, suggesting they may have stalled.
evidence: 6 of 19 items older than 30 days (31.6%)
Average age 30.0 days — mean pulled significantly above the median (17 days) by old items
P85 age 57.0 days — approaching the cycle time median of 72.9 days while still in progress
wip_age_distribution.watch_out: If any of the 6 items older than 30 days show no state change in the past 7 days, they should be explicitly surfaced in the next team meeting — items silently aging past the cycle time median are candidates for active intervention or removal from WIP.

wip_age_by_column.insight: Ageing is concentrated at the extremes of the flow: the two items in In Development have a median age of 57 days — already near the P85 cycle time — and the two items in Ready for QA have a median age of 86 days, both bugs. The single oldest item (ID 1190683, a Bug in Ready for release at 133.9 days) exceeds the maximum cycle time recorded for any completed item in the window, suggesting it may never complete without direct intervention.
evidence: In Development: median age 57 days (n=2) — approaching P85 cycle time of 126 days
Ready for QA: median age 86 days (n=2) — both are bugs
Ready for release: max age 133.9 days — beyond the observed maximum cycle time of 181 days for completed items and alarming given it is still in a pre-closure stage
wip_age_by_column.watch_out: Item 1190683 (Bug, 133.9 days in Ready for release, last updated 0.9 days ago) requires immediate investigation — it has been functionally complete for months and is awaiting a release decision that has not happened.

blockers.insight: Three items are currently blocked — all in the 'New' column and all blocked for 172.1 days — representing a chronic, unresolved condition rather than an episodic impediment. With 516.3 total days lost, these items have been stuck since well before the 6-month analysis window began. Their location in New confirms they have never progressed into active development; the blockage is at the intake/dependency layer, not within the delivery flow.
evidence: 3 current blocked items, all in New, all blocked for 172.1 days
Total days lost: 516.3 — 100% attributable to these 3 items (3 × 172.1 = 516.3)
All three last updated 144 days ago — no human action in nearly 5 months
blockers.watch_out: Items blocked for longer than the analysis window (172 days > 6-month window) have been abandoned in practice — they need a binary decision (escalate to resolve, or formally close) in the next two weeks.

blocked_by_signal.insight: All 3 currently blocked items are tagged 'Blocked'; the 'Hold' signal has 0 active items. This is a meaningful shift from April–May when Hold peaked at 5 simultaneous items, suggesting a deliberate pause was used during a planning or re-prioritisation event and has since fully cleared. Blocking is now entirely driven by genuine external impediments rather than intentional holds.
evidence: Blocked signal: 3 current items; Hold signal: 0 current items
Hold peaked at 5 items across weeks of Apr 12 through May 10
Hold has been 0 for 12 consecutive weeks since May 17
blocked_by_signal.watch_out: Confirm that the clearance of Hold items represents genuine resolution — not items having their tags silently removed. If the 5 items that were on hold in April are now closed or in active delivery, the improvement is real; if they were simply re-labelled, the underlying issues persist.

blockers_by_column.insight: All current blocked items sit in New — the pre-development intake stage — indicating that blocking is demand-side (dependencies preventing work from starting) rather than delivery-side (impediments interrupting active work). No items in Ready for Dev, In Development, In Review, or downstream stages are blocked, which suggests the delivery process itself is functioning without hard blocks, but external dependencies at the intake point are unresolved.
evidence: New: 3 blocked items; all other columns: 0 blocked
All three items have been in New for 172 days — far beyond the typical New mean dwell of 181 hours (7.5 days)
No blocked items downstream of Ready for Dev
blockers_by_column.watch_out: Verify that blocked items in New are being raised in regular planning ceremonies; if they are invisible to leadership because they sit in the backlog rather than active WIP, they will never be resolved.

blocker_timeline.insight: The 'Blocked' signal has been present every single week of the 25-week tracked period (ranging from 3 to 6 items), confirming blocking is a structural condition — not a temporary spike. The 'Hold' category showed a clear episode (late March to mid-May, peaking at 5) and has since cleared. The overall trend is decreasing, but the 3-item floor on 'Blocked' has been stable for 3 months and is unlikely to self-resolve.
evidence: Blocked present in all 25 tracked weeks — a 100% chronic rate
Hold peaked at 5 items (Apr 12–May 10), now 0 for 12 consecutive weeks
Peak combined blocked+hold: 9 items in one week; current: 3
blocker_timeline.watch_out: The stability of the Blocked count at exactly 3 for the past 12 weeks suggests these are the same 3 items — confirming they have not moved or been actioned in 3 months, not that the blocking problem is under control.

days_lost_to_blockers.insight: The 516.3 days of lost capacity is entirely attributable to 3 items each blocked for 172.1 days — their blocked time equals or exceeds their entire observable on-board history, meaning they have never had a day of active progress. These are not delays within a flow; they are items that have been parked indefinitely under a 'blocked' label.
evidence: 3 items × 172.1 days each = 516.3 days — accounts for 100% of total days lost
All three items last updated 144 days ago — no human action has been taken in response to the block
172 days blocked is equivalent to 2.4 cycle time medians — they have been stuck for longer than it takes to complete 2 typical items
days_lost_to_blockers.watch_out: If these items are closed or archived, the 'days lost' metric resets — but the underlying cause (external dependency or decision gap) needs to be documented and a recurrence prevention mechanism put in place.

stale_work.insight: 107 stale items (>30 days since last update) — 31.6% of all 339 tracked items — represent a significant hidden risk to planning accuracy, as they inflate the apparent backlog with work that may be obsolete or superseded. A suspicious cluster shows many items with exactly 144 days since last update, strongly suggesting a bulk automated or administrative event around March 16 reset timestamps without genuine human review.
evidence: 107 stale items out of 339 total tracked (31.6%)
Large cluster with exactly 144 days since last update — consistent with a single bulk event on ~Mar 16
Stale items span PBIs, Bugs, and Spikes — not concentrated in one type
stale_work.watch_out: Examine the audit log for one of the 144-day items on March 16 to confirm whether the update was a genuine review or an automated field change; if automated, these items have had no meaningful human attention in 5+ months and the true stale count may be higher than 107.

net_flow.insight: Over 26 weeks, 138 items arrived and only 79 were completed — a net deficit of 59 items. The arrival rate (5.3/week) is 77% higher than the departure rate (3.0/week), meaning the backlog grows by roughly 2.3 items every week. Excluding the Feb 16 spike (45 completions), the team has averaged approximately 1.4 completions per week against an arrival rate of 5.3 — a deeply unsustainable imbalance.
evidence: 138 arrived, 79 completed — net deficit 59 over 26 weeks
Arrival rate 5.3/week vs departure rate 3.0/week — 77% excess demand
23 of 26 weeks had negative or zero net flow
net_flow.watch_out: If the arrival rate does not decrease or the departure rate does not increase, the backlog will grow by approximately 120 items over the next 6 months — making prioritisation increasingly difficult and stakeholder commitments increasingly unreliable.

arrival_departure.insight: Most columns are in balance across the full 6-month period, and In Review is actually draining (ratio 0.84 — more departures than arrivals), suggesting the review stage has been clearing its backlog over time despite its high per-item dwell time. No column is currently accumulating at a structural rate, though the Ready for release WIP limit violations and dwell data indicate the balance here is fragile.
evidence: In Review: arrivals 148, departures 176 — ratio 0.84 (draining over 6 months)
QA: perfectly balanced (ratio 1.0, 146 in / 146 out)
No columns flagged as accumulating in this period
arrival_departure.watch_out: The period-level balance for Ready for release (ratio 0.92, 'balanced') may be misleading — at any given snapshot, Ready for release holds 3–31 items due to batchy release events; the balance averaged over time conceals the accumulation between releases.

bugs.insight: With 24 open bugs from 63 created (38% unresolved) and bugs representing 47.4% of current WIP, bug management is consuming nearly half the team's active capacity. Bug completions have occurred in isolated bursts — 6 in one week of April, 3 in early August — rather than steadily, mirroring the batch delivery pattern seen across all work types and suggesting bug resolution is not treated as a continuous daily activity.
evidence: 24 open bugs, 63 total created — 61% resolved, 39% still open
Bug share of current WIP: 47.4% (9 of 19 items)
Bug completions in only 5 distinct weeks across 26 weeks — batch pattern
bugs.watch_out: If the Jul 27 bug creation spike (8 in one week) reflects a systemic quality issue from a recent release, bug WIP share will continue rising through August — monitor weekly.

bug_intake.insight: Bug creation has been continuous throughout the 6-month window (no zero-creation weeks) at an average of ~2.4 per week, with notable spikes in late March (6 bugs, week of Mar 23) and especially late July (5 bugs Jul 20, 8 bugs Jul 27 — the highest single-week creation rate in the window). The late-July spike may correlate with a specific delivery or deployment event and warrants investigation.
evidence: 63 bugs created over ~26 weeks ≈ 2.4/week average; no weeks with zero bug creation
Spike weeks: Mar 23 (6), Jul 20 (5), Jul 27 (8) — all significantly above baseline
Jul 27 spike of 8 is 3.3× the weekly average
bug_intake.watch_out: Identify what was released or deployed in the week prior to Jul 20 and Jul 27 — if these spikes correlate with a specific feature delivery, that source component or area requires a targeted quality investigation.

bug_pct.insight: Bugs representing 47.4% of current WIP is a significant structural drain on feature delivery capacity. The 15 untriaged bugs in New represent latent demand: if all were triaged and pulled into active development, bug share would approach 60%+ and feature throughput would effectively cease. Without an explicit bug-resolution capacity allocation, the team risks permanently operating in a mostly bug-fixing mode.
evidence: Bug share of current WIP: 47.4% (9 of 19 items)
15 additional bugs in New (untriaged) — if activated, bug WIP would exceed feature WIP
Total open bugs: 24 across all columns
bug_pct.watch_out: Monitor bug share of WIP weekly; a crossing of the 50% threshold that persists for more than 2 consecutive weeks should trigger an explicit team-level conversation about feature delivery commitments.

bug_net_flow.insight: Bug creation (63) substantially outpaces closures (~39 over the window), producing a net accumulation of 24 open bugs. The two largest completion weeks (Apr 13: 6 bugs, Aug 3: 3 bugs) appear to be targeted clear-down efforts. The week of Jul 27 was the worst single-week net position for bugs — 8 created, 1 completed — suggesting the team is not keeping pace with defect injection.
evidence: 63 bugs created vs ~39 closed — net +24 open bugs
Bug completions in only 5 distinct weeks — no sustained resolution rhythm
Jul 27: 8 created, 1 completed — worst single-week deficit
bug_net_flow.watch_out: Without a consistent weekly bug resolution target, the open bug count will continue growing; a realistic target would be closing at least 3 bugs per week to eventually match the creation rate and begin drawing down the backlog.

bug_distribution.insight: 15 of 24 open bugs (62.5%) sit in New — untriaged and unstarted — suggesting most bugs are being logged but not assessed for severity, priority, or actionability. The 5 bugs in Ready for Dev are queued but not yet started. With only 1 bug in active development and 2 awaiting release, the delivery pipeline is processing bugs far more slowly than they are being created.
evidence: 15 of 24 open bugs in New (62.5% — untriaged)
5 bugs in Ready for Dev (queued but not started)
Only 1 bug in In Development — active resolution is very limited
bug_distribution.watch_out: Bugs sitting in New for more than 14 days without triage risk losing context and becoming harder to fix; a weekly bug triage ritual (30 minutes, product + engineering) would ensure severity and priority are assessed before bugs become stale.

cfd.insight: The CFD shows a growing accumulation signal: the board arrival rate (9.2 items/week entering the first column, which includes New) outpaces the departure rate (6.7/week), confirming inventory is building faster than it is resolved. The widening New band is the most prominent feature — items are entering but not progressing — while the widening Closed band confirms completions are happening, just not at a rate sufficient to match intake.
evidence: CFD arrival 9.2/week vs departure 6.7/week — net accumulation of ~2.5 items/week
Widening bands in New and Ready for Dev — intake exceeds conversion to active work
Closed band widening confirms completions are real, but insufficient to offset the accumulation
cfd.watch_out: The widening New band could reflect backlog hygiene problems (stale items never leaving New) as much as genuine new demand growth — cross-check the rate of new item creation against items formally moved out of New to distinguish the two.

wip_level_distribution.insight: Ready for release is the most structurally over-limit column: with a WIP limit of 5, it has been over that limit 41% of the time and has reached levels of 25–31 items — up to 6× the limit. In Review is similarly chronic (39.7% over limit, levels up to 30), followed by QA (27.7%) and Ready for QA (24.3%). These are not occasional violations — they are structural conditions indicating that WIP limits for downstream stages are either too low relative to batch release patterns, or are not being actively enforced.
evidence: Ready for release: 41% of days over its WIP limit of 5; observed levels up to 31
In Review: 39.7% of days over limit; levels up to 30 observed
QA: 27.7% over limit; Ready for QA: 24.3% over limit — 4 of 7 columns chronically exceed limits
wip_level_distribution.watch_out: WIP limits violated more than 25% of the time should be either enforced (with explicit stop-start rules) or honestly revised to reflect actual flow patterns — limits that exist on paper but not in practice create false confidence and prevent the team from using them as a real flow management tool.

diagnostic_findings.finding: Delivery is structurally batchy — work accumulates in review and release gates for weeks, then exits in large bursts, producing the zero-completion and spike weeks observed in throughput.
evidence: 17 of 26 weeks had zero completions; two weeks account for 58 of 79 total completions (45 + 13)
Ready for release WIP limit exceeded 41% of the time, with levels reaching 25–31 items (5–6× the limit of 5)
In Review WIP over limit 39.7% of time, with levels reaching 28–30 — large batches accumulate before clearing
diagnostic_findings.interpretation: The team's system has 'burst and pause' characteristics: work builds up in review and release gates — driven by infrequent release windows or insufficient review capacity — then clears in bulk when a release or review sprint occurs. This directly produces the zero-completion weeks and inflates cycle time for items caught in the accumulation.
plausible_explanations: Release cadence is infrequent (e.g. fortnightly or monthly), causing items to pool in Ready for release until a deployment window opens
Review capacity is insufficient relative to development output, creating a review bottleneck that periodically clears when reviewers have dedicated time
Work is intentionally coordinated across dependent items, leading to deliberate batching before release
WIP limits are not actively enforced, so there is no upstream signal to slow development when downstream stages are congested
diagnostic_findings.what_would_confirm_this: Map actual deployment dates against the Feb 16 and Apr 13 throughput spikes — if completions cluster around planned release windows, this confirms a release-cadence driver. Review the Ready for release WIP level timeline against known deployment events.

diagnostic_findings.finding: Little's Law is confirmed — the current WIP level directly determines cycle time — meaning reducing WIP is the single highest-leverage action available to improve delivery speed.
evidence: Current WIP: 19; throughput 1.8/week → Little's Law prediction 10.6 weeks; observed median cycle time 10.4 weeks — within 2%
WIP peaked at 73 in mid-February when cycle times would have been proportionally ~5–6 months
WIP declining from 73 to 19 corresponds directly to the improving cycle time trend
diagnostic_findings.interpretation: The system is predictable given its WIP level — the model is working. This means deliberate WIP reduction (not working faster, but limiting starts) will directly reduce cycle time proportionally. A reduction from 19 to 10 items would halve expected cycle time to approximately 5–6 weeks.
plausible_explanations: The team is accepting work faster than it can deliver (arrival rate 5.3/week vs departure 3.0/week), keeping WIP structurally elevated
Blocked and stale items remain in WIP counts without contributing to throughput, inflating effective WIP beyond actual active work
No whole-board WIP limit is in place — only per-column limits that are routinely exceeded
diagnostic_findings.what_would_confirm_this: Run a 4-week experiment: cap total in-progress WIP at 10 items by not starting new work until existing items close. Measure cycle time at the end.

diagnostic_findings.finding: Three items have been blocked for over 172 days with no meaningful update in 144 days — these represent a failure of impediment management, not an active delivery risk.
evidence: Items 1089190, 1092014, 1166515: all tagged Blocked, all in New, blocked 172.1 days each
516.3 total days lost — 100% from these 3 items (3 × 172.1 ≈ 516.3)
The Blocked signal has been present in all 25 tracked weeks — never resolved
diagnostic_findings.interpretation: These items are effectively abandoned. They have accumulated almost 6 months of blocked time without progress and without human intervention in nearly 5 months. Their continued presence inflates the apparent backlog and the stale-work count. They require a leadership decision to either escalate the dependency or formally close the items.
plausible_explanations: External dependencies (e.g. third-party decisions, architectural approvals, licensing) that the team cannot control and has stopped escalating
Items de-prioritised without formal closure — the 'Blocked' tag applied as a de facto parking mechanism
No individual accountable for unblocking means the items persist indefinitely in reviews
Lack of a regular blocked-item review ceremony means these are never surfaced to decision-makers
diagnostic_findings.what_would_confirm_this: Read the comments and description of items 1089190, 1092014, and 1166515 to understand the original blocker — determine whether it has been resolved without the tag being removed, or whether it remains genuinely unresolved and who owns the dependency.

diagnostic_findings.finding: Bug accumulation is consuming nearly half of active capacity, and the creation rate significantly outpaces resolution — the team is accumulating quality debt that will continue crowding out feature delivery.
evidence: 63 bugs created, ~39 closed over 26 weeks — net +24 open bugs
Bug share of current WIP: 47.4% (9 of 19 items), with 15 more untriaged in New
Bug completions in only 5 distinct weeks across the window — no sustained resolution rhythm
diagnostic_findings.interpretation: The team is in a deteriorating quality position: bugs arrive faster than they are resolved, the backlog of open bugs is growing, and nearly half of active development capacity is diverted to defect management. If unchecked, the bug share of WIP will continue rising, further crowding out product feature delivery.
plausible_explanations: Recent feature releases have introduced defects at a higher-than-historical rate (evidenced by the Jul 20 and Jul 27 spikes totalling 13 bugs in 2 weeks)
No explicit bug-resolution capacity allocation — bugs wait until a developer happens to pick one up
15 of 24 bugs are untriaged in New — without triage, severity is unknown and prioritisation is impossible
Accumulating technical quality debt is raising the defect injection rate over time
diagnostic_findings.what_would_confirm_this: Identify the feature area or release corresponding to the Jul 20 and Jul 27 bug spikes. Check whether bugs cluster around a specific component or service — if so, that area needs a focused quality intervention.

diagnostic_findings.finding: Despite genuine improvements in cycle time and lead time trends, the arrival-departure imbalance means the team's backlog is growing faster than it is being resolved — speed improvements alone cannot overcome a structural demand excess.
evidence: Cycle time trend: -6.22 days/week (improving); lead time: -11.61 days/week (improving)
Net flow: -59 items over 26 weeks — arrival 5.3/week vs departure 3.0/week
107 stale items and 339 total tracked — the backlog has grown substantially since February
diagnostic_findings.interpretation: The team is getting faster at completing individual items but is not completing enough items to match demand. This is a capacity-versus-demand problem: individual delivery is improving, but the queue for future work continues to lengthen. Stakeholders may experience faster delivery of individual items while waiting longer for their place in the queue.
plausible_explanations: Demand management is not in place — the team accepts all requests without throttling intake
The Feb 16 and Apr 13 bulk completions cleared an accumulated backlog, but new demand immediately refilled the gap
Team capacity may have reduced while demand has stayed constant
The improving cycle time trend may be recency-biased — shorter or simpler items may be being prioritised recently
diagnostic_findings.what_would_confirm_this: Review whether the volume of requests from specific stakeholders or product areas has grown over the 6-month window. Check whether team size or capacity allocation has changed since February.

diagnostic_findings.finding: WIP limits are chronically violated across four downstream stages but appear to have no enforcement consequence — they exist on paper but not as operational flow controls.
evidence: Ready for release: WIP limit 5, over limit 41% of days, observed levels up to 31
In Review: WIP limit 5, over limit 39.7% of days, levels up to 30
QA: WIP limit 3, over limit 27.7%; Ready for QA: WIP limit 3, over limit 24.3%
diagnostic_findings.interpretation: WIP limits exist on the board but are not functioning as flow controls. Violations of 2–6× the limit indicate either the limits are aspirational rather than operational, or there is no team agreement to stop pulling new work when a downstream stage is full. This perpetuates the batchy delivery pattern and prevents self-regulation.
plausible_explanations: The team has no explicit rule to block upstream starts when a downstream limit is reached
WIP limits were set historically and have not been reviewed as team capacity or work composition changed
Items in Ready for release include work pending external decisions (not just team-ready items), inflating the count beyond the team's control
The board tooling may not prominently surface WIP limit violations in real time
diagnostic_findings.what_would_confirm_this: Observe a planning or stand-up meeting — does the team check WIP levels before pulling new work? If not, the limits are nominal only. Review whether ADO board shows visual WIP limit warnings and whether they are acknowledged during ceremonies.

diagnostic_findings.finding: The primary constraint is downstream (review and release gates), not in development — investing in additional development capacity would have minimal impact on overall delivery speed.
evidence: Ready for release: mean dwell 344h, ratio 1.85× average — the identified bottleneck
In Review: mean 212.6h, median 184h — consistently slow with no extreme-outlier skew, indicating a systemic capacity problem
In Development: ratio 0.91× average — below-average dwell, confirming development is not the constraint
diagnostic_findings.interpretation: The team can build software faster than it can review and release it. The constraint is post-development. Adding developers or accelerating coding would only push more work into the already-congested In Review and Ready for release stages, worsening cycle time rather than improving it. Improvement investment should focus on review capacity and release frequency.
plausible_explanations: Review is performed by a small number of senior engineers who also have other responsibilities
The release process is manual, complex, or requires coordination with an external platform or ops team
External Review requires stakeholder availability that cannot be consistently scheduled
Items entering Ready for release are sometimes not truly release-ready (pending sign-off), inflating dwell time
diagnostic_findings.what_would_confirm_this: Measure review capacity: how many person-hours per week are available for code review and external review? Compare with the number of items transiting those stages per week. Identify whether Ready for release items are waiting for a deployment window or for a sign-off decision.

outlier_patterns.pattern: Three items have been continuously blocked in New for 172+ days with no meaningful update — effectively abandoned with no active management
evidence: All three tagged 'Blocked', blocked 172.1 days each — longer than the 6-month analysis window
Last updated 144 days ago — no human action in almost 5 months
All three remain in New column — never progressed to Ready for Dev
outlier_patterns.possible_meaning: These items represent unresolved external dependencies or decisions that the team has given up pursuing. They inflate the apparent backlog, contribute 516 days to the 'days lost to blocking' metric, and are among the 107 stale items. Their continued presence makes the active backlog appear larger and more committed than it actually is.
outlier_patterns.recommended_follow_up: Read the original blocker description and comments on each item. Escalate to whoever owns the dependency with a time-bound ask; if unresolvable within 2 weeks, formally close or move to a 'Parking Lot' state to keep the active board accurate.

outlier_patterns.pattern: The Feb 16 throughput spike (45 completions in one week) is a statistical outlier that distorts all trend calculations across the dataset
evidence: 45 completions in the week of Feb 16 vs an average of 1.8/week across the window
This single week accounts for 57% of all completions in the first 10 weeks
WIP dropped from 73 (Feb 15) to 33 (Feb 22) — a 55% reduction in one week
outlier_patterns.possible_meaning: A large batch of items was completed and closed simultaneously — possibly a sprint end, a migration from another tracking system, or a bulk administrative closure of items completed under a different process. If administrative, these completions should be excluded from throughput and trend analysis to avoid the artefact driving all trend slope calculations.
outlier_patterns.recommended_follow_up: Examine the work item history for items closed on Feb 16 — specifically what state transitions occurred and whether they were manual or automated. Ask the delivery lead what event triggered this batch. If administrative, recalculate trend metrics with this week excluded.

outlier_patterns.pattern: Two aged bugs are stranded far downstream — one in Ready for release for 133.9 days, one in Ready for QA for 86 days — each exceeding the cycle time of most completed items
evidence: Item 1190683 (Bug): 133.9 days old, in Ready for release, last updated 0.9 days ago
Item 1212553 (Bug): 86.0 days old, in Ready for QA, last updated 2 days ago
P85 cycle time for completed bugs is not available at this granularity — but completed item max was 181 days, and these items are still in-progress at 134 and 86 days respectively
outlier_patterns.possible_meaning: Item 1190683 has been functionally complete and awaiting release for over 4 months — the release decision has either not been made or is dependent on something external. Item 1212553 has been awaiting QA for nearly 3 months, suggesting a QA capacity or environment constraint. Both are consuming planning attention and WIP capacity without adding value.
outlier_patterns.recommended_follow_up: For 1190683: identify the specific release blocker — is there a deployment dependency, stakeholder approval pending, or is this awaiting a safe release window? For 1212553: check whether QA environment is available, whether the bug is still reproducible and relevant, and whether it has an assigned QA owner.

outlier_patterns.pattern: Approximately 80+ items share an exact last-updated timestamp cluster around 144 days ago — consistent with a bulk automated event rather than genuine backlog triage
evidence: Dozens of stale items show exactly 144.0 days since last update across diverse item IDs and types
144 days prior to Aug 7, 2026 = approximately March 16, 2026
Items span PBIs, Bugs, and Spikes — inconsistent with a selective human review
outlier_patterns.possible_meaning: Around March 16, a bulk operation — sprint bulk-update, board migration, area-path change, or automated process — touched all these items simultaneously, resetting their 'last updated' timestamp without genuine review. They have not been touched since, meaning no human attention in 5 months. The stale-item count may underestimate the true scale of backlog hygiene risk.
outlier_patterns.recommended_follow_up: Examine the audit history for one representative item on March 16 to determine what change was made. If it was a field update only (e.g. area path), schedule a dedicated backlog grooming session targeting all items with no meaningful content update in 90+ days.

outlier_patterns.pattern: Bug creation spike in late July (13 bugs in 2 weeks) coincides with a WIP increase — may indicate a quality issue from a recent release
evidence: Jul 20: 5 bugs created; Jul 27: 8 bugs created — 13 in 2 weeks vs average ~2.4/week (5.4× baseline)
WIP increased from 7 (Jul 19) to 18 (Aug 2) in the same period
Week of Jul 27 is the highest single-week bug creation in the entire 6-month window
outlier_patterns.possible_meaning: A release or deployment event in mid-to-late July introduced a higher-than-usual defect rate. The simultaneous WIP increase suggests the team is now managing both the new bugs and normal feature work, putting pressure on delivery capacity. If the spike is concentrated in a specific feature area, that component has elevated defect injection.
outlier_patterns.recommended_follow_up: Identify what was deployed or released in the week before Jul 20. Review the descriptions of the ~13 bugs created in those 2 weeks to determine whether they cluster around a specific feature area, component, or service. If so, consider a focused quality investigation or additional testing investment for that area.

outlier_patterns.pattern: Apr 13 throughput spike (13 completions) followed by 6 consecutive weeks of near-zero completions — a secondary instance of the batch-release pattern
evidence: Apr 13: 13 completions; Apr 20 through May 25: 0, 0, 0, 1, 0 completions
WIP dropped from 58 (Apr 12) to 23 (Apr 19) in one week following the batch
This mirrors the Feb 16 pattern — large batch followed by weeks of zero completions
outlier_patterns.possible_meaning: A second planned batch release cleared accumulated work in mid-April, followed by a 'restart' cycle where the team pulled in new work without completing it for several weeks. This confirms the system operates in planned-batch mode rather than continuous pull, with structural release cadence driving the delivery rhythm.
outlier_patterns.recommended_follow_up: Confirm whether Apr 13 corresponded to a planned sprint end or release window. If so, explore whether a shorter cadence (e.g. weekly releases, or continuous deployment) is feasible — this would smooth throughput, reduce cycle time, and eliminate zero-completion weeks.

executive_summary.headline: The team is genuinely getting faster at delivering individual pieces of work, but is accepting requests nearly twice as fast as it can complete them — the backlog is growing, nearly half of active effort is now consumed by bug fixes, and work moves in large batches rather than as a steady, predictable stream.
executive_summary.narrative: Over the past six months, the Analytics and Experimentation team has made real progress: individual items are being completed somewhat faster than they were earlier in the year, and the volume of active work-in-progress has roughly halved from its February peak. However, for every 3 requests the team completes each week, it receives more than 5 new ones — meaning the queue of outstanding work grows by roughly 2 items every week and will continue to do so without a change to how demand is managed. Delivery tends to happen in large bursts — two weeks accounted for the majority of all completions over the six-month period — rather than as a steady, predictable stream, which makes it difficult for stakeholders to plan with confidence. Nearly half of the team's current active effort is consumed by bug fixes rather than new product features, and three items have been marked as externally blocked for over five months without any progress or intervention — suggesting the team needs stronger support in managing dependencies and resolving impediments. The most significant bottlenecks are not in the development phase itself, but in review and release stages: completed work often waits one to two weeks or longer before reaching users, not because it is unfinished, but because deployment opportunities are infrequent.
executive_summary.primary_diagnosis: The team is supply-constrained relative to demand, with structural review and release bottlenecks slowing completed work to users, while bug accumulation and unmanaged blockers consume capacity that should be available for product delivery.
executive_summary.main_caveat: The Feb 16 bulk completion event (45 items in one week) is likely an anomaly that distorts trend calculations, and the cycle time and lead time samples cover partially different populations of items; all trend-direction conclusions should be treated as directional rather than definitive until 2–3 more months of clean, steady-state data are available.

investigate_next.question: What caused the Feb 16 batch of 45 completions — was it a genuine delivery event, a planned sprint closure, or a bulk administrative update of stale items?

investigate_next.decision_it_would_inform: Whether the 'throughput worsening' trend label is valid; whether historical cycle times are genuinely comparable to recent ones; whether reported metrics should exclude this week.

investigate_next.data_or_conversation_needed: Read the descriptions, comments, and history for all three items. Identify the named owner. Present to the next leadership review with a binary ask: 'What would it take to unblock this in the next 2 weeks — or should it be formally closed?'
investigate_next.decision_it_would_inform: Whether to unblock (requiring escalation of a specific external dependency) or formally close these items and clear the backlog; also informs whether a regular blocked-item review ceremony is needed.

investigate_next.question: What prevents items from being released once they reach Ready for release — is it release cadence, a sign-off process, or a deployment pipeline dependency?
investigate_next.why_it_matters: Ready for release is the confirmed bottleneck with a mean dwell of 344 hours, exceeded 41% of the time with observed levels up to 31 items. Addressing this has the largest single potential impact on cycle time of any intervention available.
investigate_next.data_or_conversation_needed: Map actual deployment dates against the Ready for release WIP level over time. Ask the team: 'What has to happen before an item in Ready for release can be deployed?' Identify who owns the release decision and whether there is a deployment window constraint.
investigate_next.decision_it_would_inform: Whether to increase release frequency, automate the release pipeline, restructure sign-off criteria, or negotiate a more frequent deployment cadence with the platform team.

investigate_next.question: What does In Review require before an item can pass through — who performs reviews, and how is review capacity allocated relative to development output?
investigate_next.why_it_matters: In Review has a mean dwell of 212.6 hours (nearly 9 days on average), is over its WIP limit 39.7% of the time, and has accumulated up to 30 items simultaneously. If review is performed by a small number of senior engineers, this is a direct capacity bottleneck limiting total team throughput.
investigate_next.data_or_conversation_needed: Review the ADO history for items in In Review — who is assigned as reviewer? How many people review regularly? Are items sitting with no reviewer assigned? Check whether In Review covers code review only or also includes design and product reviews as unstated substeps.
investigate_next.decision_it_would_inform: Whether to add review capacity (pair review, dedicated review slots), change the review process, or split In Review into explicit substages with separate WIP limits.

investigate_next.question: Are the WIP limits on the board actively enforced in team ceremonies, or are they informational only?
investigate_next.why_it_matters: Four of seven in-progress columns exceed their WIP limits more than 24% of the time. If limits do not trigger 'stop starting, start finishing' conversations, they provide no flow management benefit and their existence creates false confidence.
investigate_next.data_or_conversation_needed: Observe the next planning or flow review meeting and note whether WIP levels are checked before new work is pulled. Ask the team: 'What is our rule when a column is at its WIP limit?' Review whether the board tooling surfaces WIP limit violations prominently.
investigate_next.decision_it_would_inform: Whether to keep current limits and enforce them with an explicit stop rule, revise them to reflect actual capacity, or introduce a whole-board WIP cap as a more effective alternative to per-column limits.

investigate_next.question: Is the team's demand intake actively controlled, or is all requested work being accepted regardless of current capacity?
investigate_next.why_it_matters: Arrival rate (5.3 items/week) is 77% higher than departure rate (3.0/week). No amount of speed improvement can overcome a structural imbalance of this magnitude without also throttling intake. The backlog will grow indefinitely otherwise.
investigate_next.data_or_conversation_needed: Ask the product manager or delivery lead: 'How do we decide what goes on the board and when — is there a capacity limit on how many items we accept per week?' Review whether there is a defined readiness gate before items enter New or Ready for Dev.
investigate_next.decision_it_would_inform: Whether to implement an explicit intake policy (e.g. no more than X new items per week, or only accept items when WIP is below Y), and whether demand reduction should be negotiated with stakeholders.

investigate_next.question: What is the true quality and relevance of the 107 stale items in the backlog — and should any be formally closed?
investigate_next.why_it_matters: 107 stale items (31.6% of the tracked set) create planning noise, inflate backlog size, and may have been superseded by newer work. The cluster updated exactly 144 days ago likely reflects an automated event rather than genuine review — these items have had no human attention in 5+ months.
investigate_next.data_or_conversation_needed: Export all items in New with last-updated > 90 days. Schedule a 2-hour grooming session with product manager and delivery lead. For each item: still needed? Superseded? Can it be closed? Verify the audit history of the March 16 bulk update.
investigate_next.decision_it_would_inform: What the true active backlog size is — which directly determines realistic capacity planning and whether the team is over-committed to stakeholders.

recommendations.action: Establish a whole-board WIP cap and enforce it as the first check in every planning or stand-up meeting — no new items start until total in-progress WIP is below an agreed limit
recommendations.why: Little's Law confirms that current WIP (19 items) directly determines cycle time (~10 weeks). Reducing WIP is the single highest-leverage action to improve delivery speed without changing team size. Per-column limits exist but are violated routinely without consequence.
recommendations.first_step: In the next retrospective, agree a whole-board WIP limit of 12–14 items. Add a WIP count check as the first item in any planning ceremony — if WIP is at the cap, the rule is 'finish before starting'. Post the current WIP count visibly (e.g. on a shared dashboard or board header).
recommendations.metric_to_watch: Cycle time median and WIP over time
recommendations.expected_effect: A sustained reduction from 19 to 12 WIP items should reduce median cycle time from ~73 days to approximately 45–50 days within 6–8 weeks, per Little's Law.

recommendations.action: Increase release cadence or reduce release batch size to prevent work accumulating in Ready for release
recommendations.why: Ready for release is the confirmed bottleneck: mean dwell 344 hours, exceeded 41% of the time with levels reaching 31 items. This is where completed work waits to reach users. More frequent releases would reduce average wait time for items that are functionally done.
recommendations.first_step: Map the last 3 months of actual deployments against the Ready for release WIP level. Identify whether release windows could be made more frequent (e.g. weekly instead of fortnightly). Engage the platform or ops team to understand deployment pipeline constraints and what would be needed to release more often.
recommendations.metric_to_watch: Ready for release mean dwell time and WIP level distribution
recommendations.expected_effect: Doubling release frequency would approximately halve mean dwell in Ready for release, reducing overall cycle time by an estimated 1–2 weeks per item.

recommendations.action: Triage the three long-blocked items (1089190, 1092014, 1166515) within 2 weeks — either escalate to resolve the blocker or formally close them
recommendations.why: These items have been blocked for 172 days with no update in 144 days. They represent 516 days of lost capacity, inflate the backlog, and distort all blocked-item metrics. A binary decision is needed: act or close.
recommendations.first_step: Assign a specific person (delivery lead or product manager) to review all three items this week. Read the original blocker description and comments. Present a binary choice for each at the next leadership meeting: 'What specific action would resolve this in 2 weeks?' If no actionable answer exists, close the item with a note explaining why.
recommendations.metric_to_watch: Currently blocked item count and total days lost to blocking
recommendations.expected_effect: Immediate reduction in blocked-item count to 0 (if all closed), clearing 516 days from the blocking metric; also removes 3 items from the stale backlog count.

recommendations.action: Implement a weekly bug triage ritual and reserve explicit capacity for bug resolution each sprint
recommendations.why: Bugs are arriving at ~2.4/week, 15 of 24 open bugs are untriaged in New, and bug share of WIP is 47.4%. Without explicit capacity allocation and triage, bugs accumulate and progressively crowd out feature delivery.
recommendations.first_step: In the next sprint or planning session: (1) assign severity to all 15 untriaged bugs in New (15-minute triage pass), (2) reserve 20–25% of developer capacity for bug resolution, (3) set a standing rule that no new feature work starts while more than 5 bugs are in the active flow. Review the Jul 20 and Jul 27 bug spike to identify whether a specific component needs targeted attention.
recommendations.metric_to_watch: Bug share of WIP and bug net flow (bugs closed minus bugs created per week)
recommendations.expected_effect: Within 4–6 weeks, bug WIP share should reduce below 30%, freeing capacity for feature work and stabilising the open bug count.

recommendations.action: Address the In Review bottleneck by measuring review capacity and introducing a 'review before starting' norm when In Review is at its WIP limit
recommendations.why: In Review has a mean dwell of 212.6 hours, is over its WIP limit 39.7% of the time, and has reached levels of 28–30 items. This is the primary internal delivery bottleneck and is driven by review capacity, not development pace.
recommendations.first_step: In the next retrospective, map who performs reviews and with what frequency. Introduce a team norm: if In Review is at or above 5 items, developers complete a review before pulling new work into development. This redistributes review capacity from concentrated individuals to the full team.
recommendations.metric_to_watch: In Review mean dwell time and WIP level
recommendations.expected_effect: If consistent reviewer availability is achieved, reducing In Review WIP from its typical 5–12 items to consistently below 5 would reduce average time in this stage from ~212 hours to approximately 40–60 hours — a saving of approximately 1 week per item.

recommendations.action: Run a focused backlog grooming session targeting all items last updated more than 90 days ago, with the explicit aim of closing or archiving at least 50%
recommendations.why: 107 stale items (31.6% of the tracked board) create a misleading picture of committed work, inflate backlog size, and make capacity planning unreliable. The cluster of items updated exactly 144 days ago likely reflects an automated event — these have had no genuine review in 5 months.
recommendations.first_step: Export all items in the New column with last-updated > 90 days. Schedule a 2-hour session with product manager and delivery lead within the next 2 weeks. Apply a simple rule to each item: 'Still needed and started within 60 days? Keep. Otherwise, close with a brief note.' Target: reduce the New column from its current ~160 average items to under 80.
recommendations.metric_to_watch: Stale item count and New column average WIP in the CFD
recommendations.expected_effect: A cleaner backlog will improve prioritisation accuracy, may reduce the effective arrival rate (as some stale items generate false demand), and provides stakeholders with an honest picture of team commitments.

recommendations.action: Introduce explicit demand management — limit new items entering the active flow each week to a rate the team can realistically complete
recommendations.why: Arrival rate (5.3 items/week) is 77% higher than departure rate (3.0/week), generating a net deficit of ~2.3 items every week. No delivery speed improvement can overcome a structural arrival-departure imbalance of this magnitude without also controlling intake.
recommendations.first_step: Agree with product management on a sustainable intake policy — for example, 'no more than 3–4 new items per week enter Ready for Dev'. Create a visible intake queue reviewed weekly with explicit prioritisation decisions, rather than implicit acceptance of all requests. Communicate the constraint to stakeholders proactively with expected queue wait times.
recommendations.metric_to_watch: Weekly net flow (arrival vs departure rate) and backlog size over time
recommendations.expected_effect: If arrival rate is reduced to match departure rate (~3.0/week), the backlog will stabilise within 4 weeks and begin shrinking within 8 weeks, improving predictability and reducing the pressure that keeps WIP chronically elevated.

data_quality_caveats: The Feb 16, 2026 throughput spike (45 completions in one week against an average of 1.8/week) is a statistical outlier that materially distorts throughput trend slopes, cycle time distributions, and WIP trend calculations. If this was a bulk administrative closure rather than a genuine delivery event, all trend-dependent metrics should be recalculated with this week excluded before acting on trend-direction conclusions.

The cycle time sample (48 items) and lead time sample (30 items) appear to cover partially different item populations — this is the most likely explanation for median cycle time (72.9 days) being longer than median lead time (39.1 days), which would be theoretically impossible for the same item given that cycle time starts later (Ready for Dev) than lead time (New). Cross-metric comparisons between lead time and cycle time should be interpreted with caution.

96 items were excluded from analysis due to an unknown historical swimlane ('Data Layer'), representing approximately 28% of the 339 total tracked items. If these items had systematically different cycle times, completion rates, or work types, the reported metrics may not represent the full team workflow. This exclusion affects all metrics proportionally.

The three currently blocked items (1089190, 1092014, 1166515) have been blocked for 172+ days — longer than the 6-month analysis window. Their full blocked duration is unknown; the 516.3 days lost figure is a lower bound, not the true total time lost.

A large cluster of stale items share an exact or near-exact 'last updated' timestamp of 144 days ago (approximately March 16, 2026), consistent with a bulk automated field change rather than genuine human review. If this is confirmed, the stale item count and backlog hygiene assessment may underestimate the true scale of the problem, as these items have had no meaningful review despite their timestamp appearing recently updated.
Work start efficiency is calculated on only 14 items — too small a sample to draw firm conclusions. This metric should be treated as directional only until the sample reaches at least 30 items.

Flow efficiency is calculated across 106 items spanning both the high-WIP period (Feb–Apr, with WIP of 33–73) and the lower-WIP period (May–Aug, with WIP of 7–19). The mean and median efficiency figures may not represent the current system state. A filtered view of the most recent 8 weeks would provide a more relevant picture of today's flow.

The 6-month analysis window may be insufficient to distinguish genuine trend changes from seasonal variation, team composition changes, or the effect of specific one-time events (the Feb 16 and Apr 13 batch releases). Trend conclusions about cycle time and lead time improving should be monitored for a further 2–3 months before being treated as sustained structural improvements.
